transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I’m here because things kind of blew up at work, and I don’t think I can keep pretending it was just a misunderstanding or normal pressure.

I work in HR, and we had this onboarding launch—new process, vendors involved, company money involved, approvals that were supposed to happen in a certain order. And I just… pushed it forward anyway. At the time it honestly felt like the right thing to do, like I was cutting through red tape and being decisive, and I remember thinking, “Someone has to move this along.” I committed vendor time and company resources before everything was signed off, and I didn’t see it as reckless in the moment. I saw it as bold, necessary, even helpful.

But now I’m on leave, and people are asking what I was thinking, and I don’t have a good answer that makes sense to them—or honestly, to me now. It’s embarrassing and stressful, and I’m here because the consequences are real, and I need to understand why I thought that was okay at the time.
Have you ever done something similar like this before at work or in other areas of your life?

The clearest example is the one that brought me here, honestly. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m dodging the question, but this work situation is the thing that’s really standing out because it had actual consequences.

With the onboarding launch, I pushed it forward before the approvals were in place. I committed vendor time and company money, and at the time I really did not experience it as “I’m breaking process” or “I’m taking a risk that could come back on me.” It felt almost the opposite, like I was finally moving something that everyone else was too slow or too cautious to handle. In my head it was bold, necessary, like I was being the person willing to make the decision.

And now, sitting here, I can see why people are asking what I was thinking. I’m on leave because of it, and everyone is looking at the choices I made like they were obviously out of bounds. I guess what scares me is that in the moment it didn’t feel out of bounds to me. It felt justified. So yes, something like this has happened—this is the big one I can point to—and I’m still trying to understand how I got so convinced it was the right thing to do.
Do you often find yourself disregarding rules or social norms in your personal life, outside of work?

I’m not sure I’d say “often,” no. At least, I don’t think of myself that way in my personal life. I mean, I’m not someone who goes around intentionally breaking rules or trying to shock people or ignoring basic expectations just because I don’t care.

That said, I’m hesitating because after what happened at work, I don’t fully trust my own read on myself. Like, if you had asked me before this whole thing whether I was the type of person to bypass approvals and commit company resources without sign-off, I probably would have said absolutely not. So when you ask about rules or social norms outside of work, part of me wants to say, “No, that’s not me,” but another part is thinking, well, maybe I don’t always recognize it in the moment.

In my personal life, I don’t have some clear pattern jumping out at me. I’m not thinking of repeated examples where people are always telling me I crossed lines or broke norms. If there are smaller things, I may be missing them, but nothing as obvious as the work situation. So I guess my honest answer is: not that I’ve noticed, but I’m not feeling very confident in my judgment right now.
Do you often feel like you're more important or special than others?

I don’t know if I’d put it that way exactly. “More important or special than others” sounds so stark, like I’m walking around thinking I’m above people, and I don’t think that’s how I see myself day to day.

But I’m also trying to be careful, because in that work situation I clearly thought my judgment mattered more than the process, or at least more than waiting for everyone else to sign off. At the time it didn’t feel like arrogance in my head. It felt like urgency, like I understood what needed to happen and other people were getting in the way or being too slow. So if you’re asking whether I sometimes get convinced that I’m the one who sees things correctly and should be able to act on it… maybe, yes, in that situation.

I don’t have a general feeling like I’m better than everyone else. I don’t walk into rooms thinking people should defer to me. But I can see how, from the outside, some of my thinking probably looked like I had given myself permission that other people didn’t have. That’s hard to admit, but it’s probably the most honest answer I can give.
Do you often expect special treatment or automatic compliance from others?

I don’t think I “often” expect special treatment, no. At least not in the obvious sense of thinking rules shouldn’t apply to me or that people should just automatically do what I say because I said it.

I mean, in normal personal situations, I don’t think I’m walking around expecting people to rearrange themselves around me. I wait in lines, I make appointments, I don’t usually demand exceptions or anything like that. And at work, under normal circumstances, I’d like to believe I respect procedures and people’s roles.

But I’m also hearing the word “automatic compliance,” and I feel a little uncomfortable because with the work situation, I guess I did act like people should catch up to what I had already decided. I don’t remember thinking, “Everyone should obey me,” but I was definitely impatient with the idea that other people needed to approve things before they happened. It felt like if I could see the path clearly, then other people should be able to see it too, and if they didn’t, they were slowing things down.

So… I wouldn’t say this is a broad pattern I recognize in myself. I don’t think I generally expect special treatment. But I can see that in that situation, my behavior probably looked like I expected the normal checks not to apply to me, or like I expected others to go along with my decision after the fact. That’s probably the most honest way I can answer it.
Do you often find yourself seeking praise or admiration from others for your actions or decisions?

I’m not sure. I don’t think I’m someone who is constantly fishing for compliments, if that’s what you mean. I don’t usually do things just so people will praise me, at least not consciously.

But I suppose I do care how my actions are seen. I mean, most people do, right? If I make a decision and I think it was a good one, especially if it took effort or judgment, then yes, part of me probably wants other people to recognize that. I wouldn’t say I need admiration exactly, but I do notice whether people seem to respect my judgment.

With the situation we’ve been talking about, it’s hard to separate things out. At the time, I don’t remember thinking, “Everyone will admire me for this.” It felt more like I believed I was doing the right thing and expected people to understand that once they saw the outcome. Maybe there was some wish to be seen as decisive or capable, but I don’t know that I’d call it seeking praise.

So I guess my answer is: not often, not in a deliberate way that I’m aware of. I like being appreciated, and I probably feel hurt or defensive if I think something I did is being misunderstood, but I don’t think I’m usually chasing admiration.
Do you often use charm or manipulation to get what you want from others?

I don’t think so, at least not in the way I understand those words. “Manipulation” feels pretty intentional to me, like you know exactly what someone wants to hear and you use that to steer them without being honest. I don’t think I do that as a pattern.

Charm is a little harder, because I work with people, and I can be diplomatic. I try to phrase things in a way that people can hear, and I may try to smooth things over or make a case for something. But I don’t think of that as charm in a calculated way. It’s more like trying to communicate effectively, or trying not to make a situation worse.

I guess if I want something, I can be persuasive. I can explain why I think it makes sense, and I probably keep talking longer than I need to sometimes. But I’m not aware of using people, or flattering them just to get my way, or pretending to be someone I’m not so they’ll agree with me.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed that in myself. If other people experience me that way, I suppose I’d want to know, but from the inside it doesn’t feel like I’m manipulating people.
Do you often act on impulse without fully considering the consequences of your actions?

Yes… I mean, I don’t like saying “often,” because I don’t think I’m impulsive in every part of my life. I’m not usually someone who just does reckless things for no reason. But if you’re asking whether I acted without fully thinking through the consequences in the situation that brought me here, then yes. I think I have to say yes.

The clearest example is the onboarding launch. I pushed ahead with it before all the approvals were actually in place. At the time it didn’t feel impulsive to me. That’s the strange part. It felt bold, decisive, necessary — like if I waited for every sign-off and every committee discussion, the whole thing would lose momentum and everyone would later agree I had been right to move it forward.

But looking back, I committed company money and vendor time before I really had the authority to do that. I can say now that I did not sit with the consequences properly. I didn’t really think through what would happen if leadership didn’t back me, or if finance objected, or if the vendor started work and then people asked who approved it. I sort of assumed the outcome would justify the decision.

And now I’m on leave, and everyone is basically asking, “What were you thinking?” Which is painful, because at the time I thought I was solving a problem, not creating one. So yes, in that situation, I acted first and understood the consequences later.
Do you often feel entitled to special treatment or automatic obedience from others because of your intelligence, talent, or accomplishments?

I don’t think I feel entitled to special treatment, no. At least, I don’t walk around thinking rules shouldn’t apply to me because I’m smart or because I’ve done good work. That sounds ugly when I say it that way, and I really don’t believe that’s how I usually see myself.

I do think I get frustrated when I feel like people aren’t listening to reason, or when a process seems slow or overly cautious. And maybe in those moments I can come across as if I think my judgment should carry more weight than everyone else’s. I can see that possibility. But from the inside, it doesn’t feel like, “I’m special, so obey me.” It feels more like, “I’ve thought this through, why are we getting stuck?”

Automatic obedience… no, that doesn’t sound right. I don’t expect people to just follow me blindly. I actually prefer when people understand the reasoning. I can get impatient when they don’t, or when I think the objections are more procedural than substantive, but that’s different from expecting obedience because of who I am.

So I guess my answer is: not usually, no. I may overestimate how obvious my reasoning is, or feel offended if my competence is questioned, but I don’t think I generally believe I deserve special treatment just because of my intelligence or accomplishments.
Do you often feel like your opinions or ideas are more valuable or important than those of others?

I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly. I mean, I do have opinions, and when I’ve thought something through carefully, I can feel pretty convinced that I’m right. Sometimes probably too convinced, if I’m being honest. But “more valuable or important than other people’s” sounds like I’m dismissing everyone else as irrelevant, and I don’t think that’s how I generally operate.

I usually want to hear what other people think, especially if they have information I don’t have. I can get frustrated, though, when I feel like an idea is being rejected for reasons that don’t seem substantive to me, or when the conversation feels like it’s going in circles. Then I might push harder and talk too much, and I can see how that might make it seem like I think my view matters more.

From the inside, it feels less like “my ideas are inherently better” and more like, “I believe this particular idea makes sense, and I’m trying to get people to see why.” But I guess the effect can still be that I crowd out other people’s perspectives. I don’t like that possibility, but I can recognize it.

So… not as a general belief, no. I don’t think my opinions are automatically more important just because they’re mine. But when I’m convinced of something, I may act like they are more important in that moment, even if I don’t mean to.
Have you ever taken advantage of someone's trust or naivety for your own gain?

No… I don’t think so. At least, not in the sense of deliberately looking at someone and thinking, “They trust me, so I can use that.” That would feel really awful to me.

I’ve definitely benefited from people trusting me at work — people assuming I know what I’m doing, giving me room to make decisions, not questioning every little thing — but I don’t think I’ve consciously exploited that for personal gain. And “naivety” especially… I don’t think I target people who are less experienced or easier to persuade. I mean, I hope I don’t.

I suppose there may have been times when I was persuasive and got people to go along with something because I believed I was right, and maybe they trusted my judgment more than they should have. But that’s different, at least in my mind, from taking advantage of them. I wasn’t trying to get something out of them for myself.

So my answer would be no, not that I’m aware of. If someone else felt used by me, I’d want to know that, but I don’t recognize that as a pattern in myself.
Do you generally believe you are more capable of making important decisions than most other people?

I don’t know that I generally believe that, no. I mean, “important decisions” is a big category. If it’s something in an area I know well, or something where I’ve really done the work and looked at the consequences, then yes, I might trust my judgment more than I trust the average off-the-cuff opinion. But that’s not the same as thinking I’m more capable than most people across the board.

I work with people, so I see all the time that different people are good at different kinds of decisions. Some people are better at reading the emotional side of a situation, some are better at legal or procedural details, some are better at stepping back when things get heated. I don’t think I’m superior at all of that. If anything, I can sometimes get too locked into what seems logical to me and miss that someone else is seeing a different piece of the picture.

That said, I probably do have a lot of confidence in my own reasoning when I feel informed. Maybe more confidence than is always helpful. I can think, “Why are we overcomplicating this?” or “This seems obvious,” and then later realize it wasn’t obvious to everyone because they were weighing things differently. So I guess I’d say I trust myself, sometimes strongly, but I don’t walk around believing I’m inherently better than most people at making major decisions.
Do you often find yourself exaggerating your achievements or talents to others?

I don’t think I often exaggerate, no. I mean… I might present things in the best light, especially at work, because that’s sort of part of how people talk about accomplishments. Like if I’ve led a project, I’ll say I led it, but I try not to make it sound like I single-handedly did everything if other people were involved.

I’m actually a little careful about that, because in HR you hear people describe their performance or their conflict with someone, and you can tell when they’re inflating their role or leaving out context. So I’m conscious of not wanting to be that person. At least, I hope I’m not.

That said, I probably do emphasize the parts I’m proud of. If I’m in an interview-type situation or trying to explain why I handled something well, I might highlight my judgment or experience. But I don’t think I invent achievements or claim talents I don’t have. I’d be too worried about being caught out, honestly, and it would feel embarrassing.

So… not often, I’d say. Maybe I polish the wording sometimes, but I don’t see myself as someone who exaggerates in a major way.
Do you often feel like you deserve special treatment because of your accomplishments or status?

I don’t think so, not in a broad sense. I mean, I think everyone likes to be recognized for work they’ve done, and I’m not immune to that. If I’ve put a lot into something and it goes well, I do appreciate people noticing, or at least not acting like it was nothing. But “special treatment” feels like a stronger thing.

I don’t think I walk into situations feeling like rules shouldn’t apply to me because of my job title or because I’ve accomplished certain things. If anything, because I work in HR, I’m pretty aware of how bad that looks — when someone thinks their seniority or reputation means they should get exceptions everyone else wouldn’t get. That kind of thing bothers me.

Now, I might expect a certain level of respect or professional courtesy, especially if I’ve earned trust over time. Like, if I’ve handled sensitive situations well before, I might feel frustrated if someone suddenly treats me like I don’t know what I’m doing. But I see that as wanting my experience to count for something, not wanting to be above other people.

I guess there are moments where I think, “Come on, I’ve been doing this long enough, I shouldn’t have to prove every little thing.” But I don’t think that’s the same as deserving special treatment. It’s more wanting not to be dismissed. So… no, I wouldn’t say I often feel that way.
Do you often have difficulty understanding why others are upset or offended by your actions?

I wouldn’t say often, no. I mean, I can usually understand it once someone explains what landed badly. Especially because of my work, I spend a lot of time thinking about tone, impact, how something might be received, whether someone felt dismissed or embarrassed. So it’s not like I’m completely oblivious to that kind of thing.

But there are definitely times where my first reaction is more like, “Wait, why did that upset you?” Not because I think they have no right to be upset, but because in my head I’m focused on the intent. Like if I was trying to solve a problem or be direct, I may not immediately see that the way I said it came across as critical or impatient. Then if they tell me, I can usually back up and say, okay, I can see how that sounded.

I think I’m better at understanding it after the fact than in the moment. In the moment, I might be a little too caught up in the practical side — what needs to happen, what decision needs to be made, what the policy is, that sort of thing. And then later I’ll replay it and realize, “Oh, they weren’t reacting to the content, they were reacting to feeling talked over,” or something like that.

So… difficulty, sometimes. Often, I don’t think so. I’m not always as quick as I’d like to be, but I usually can get there if I slow down or if the person tells me directly.
Do you find it hard to put yourself in other people's shoes and understand their feelings?

I don’t think I find it hard in a general way, no. I mean, part of my job is almost literally trying to understand where different people are coming from, even when they’re upset or when I don’t personally agree with them. I have to think about, okay, what did this feel like from their side, what might they be worried about, are they feeling disrespected, embarrassed, threatened, ignored — all of that.

That said, I’m probably better at doing it when I have time to step back and think. In the moment, especially if things are tense or someone is being emotional in a way that feels unfair to me, I can get a little too focused on the facts. Like, “Here’s what happened, here’s the policy, here’s what I meant,” and I may not immediately slow down enough to really sit with how it felt for them. Later, I can usually see it more clearly.

So I wouldn’t say I’m unable to put myself in someone else’s shoes. I do care how people feel, and I can usually understand it if I stop and think or if they tell me directly. But I’m not perfect at it in real time. Sometimes I need a minute to get out of my own perspective first.
Do you think you have trouble understanding and sharing the feelings of others?

I mean… I’m not sure I’d describe it as trouble understanding or sharing feelings, at least not as a general pattern. I do try to understand what other people are feeling, and I don’t think I’m cold to it. If someone is upset in front of me, I usually do care, even if I’m also trying to figure out what actually happened or what needs to be done.

I guess where I hesitate is the “sharing” part, because I don’t always feel things in the same way someone else does. Like, I can understand that someone feels hurt or embarrassed or anxious without necessarily feeling it right along with them. Sometimes I’m more analytical at first — I’m thinking, okay, what led to this, what can I do, what do they need from me — and then the emotional part catches up a little later.

So… not usually, no. But I can be slower with it in the moment than I’d like. If I’m stressed or trying to solve something, I may come across more practical than warm, and I can see how someone might experience that as me not getting it. I don’t think that means I don’t understand or care, but I probably don’t always show it right away.
Do you usually consider how your actions might affect the feelings of others before you do something?

Usually, yes — or at least I try to. I think I probably consider it more in some settings than others. At work, for example, I’m very aware that what I say or how I say it can affect people. If I’m sending an email, having a difficult conversation, giving feedback, dealing with a complaint, I’ll often think through how it might land. Like, will this make the person feel blamed, or cornered, or dismissed? Am I being clear without sounding harsh? That kind of thing.

In my personal life, I do think about it too, but maybe not always as deliberately. If I’m tired or focused on getting something done, I can be more blunt than I intend, and I may not fully think through the emotional impact until afterward. Then I’ll sort of replay it and think, “Okay, that may have sounded sharper than I meant,” or “I probably should’ve said that differently.”

So I wouldn’t say I go around not caring how people feel. I do care. But I’m not always perfect at anticipating it before I act. Sometimes I’m better at recognizing it after the fact, especially if someone reacts strongly or tells me directly.
Have you ever used your position or influence to influence someone's decision for your own benefit?

I’m trying to think how to answer that honestly, because “position or influence” can mean a lot of things. In my work, technically I do have some influence in situations — not like I’m the final authority on everything, but people may take what I say seriously because of my role. So I’m pretty aware that I have to be careful with that.

Have I used it for my own benefit? I don’t think so, not in a manipulative way. I mean, I’ve probably advocated for something that made my life easier, like suggesting a process or pushing for a decision that I thought would reduce problems later, including problems for me. But I wouldn’t say I’ve pressured someone or taken advantage of my role to get something personal out of it.

If you mean something like steering someone’s decision so I get a favor, or avoid consequences, or get special treatment — no, I don’t think that’s something I do. I’d actually be pretty uncomfortable with that, because in HR especially, that kind of thing can get unethical very quickly. I’m sure I have opinions and biases like anyone does, but I try not to use my role that way.
Do you often find it difficult to understand why someone would feel a certain way in a situation?

Not often, no. I mean, I can usually come up with a reason why someone might feel the way they do, even if I wouldn’t feel the same way in that exact situation. A lot of the time it’s kind of… I look at the circumstances, what the person values, what they might be afraid of, what history might be there, and then it makes sense enough.

There are times I don’t get it right away, though. Especially if someone has what seems to me like a very intense reaction to something I would see as minor, or if they don’t explain what part of it upset them. Then I might think, “Wait, why is this such a big deal?” But usually if I slow down and ask a few questions, or think about it from their angle, I can understand it better.

So I wouldn’t say it’s a frequent difficulty. It’s more that sometimes my first reaction is practical or logical, and the emotional reasoning takes a minute to catch up. But I’m not usually just baffled by other people’s feelings.

I don’t remember thinking, “Everyone should obey me,” but I was definitely impatient with the idea that other people needed to approve things before they happened. It felt like if I could see the path clearly, then other people should be able to see it too, and if they didn’t, they were slowing things down.

So… I wouldn’t say this is a broad pattern I recognize in myself. I don’t think I generally expect special treatment. But I can see that in that situation, my behavior probably looked like I expected the normal checks not to apply to me, or like I expected others to go along with my decision after the fact. That’s probably the most honest way I can answer it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a consistent need for admiration

But I suppose I do care how my actions are seen. I mean, most people do, right? If I make a decision and I think it was a good one, especially if it took effort or judgment, then yes, part of me probably wants other people to recognize that. I wouldn’t say I need admiration exactly, but I do notice whether people seem to respect my judgment.

With the situation we’ve been talking about, it’s hard to separate things out. At the time, I don’t remember thinking, “Everyone will admire me for this.” It felt more like I believed I was doing the right thing and expected people to understand that once they saw the outcome. Maybe there was some wish to be seen as decisive or capable, but I don’t know that I’d call it seeking praise.

So I guess my answer is: not often, not in a deliberate way that I’m aware of. I like being appreciated, and I probably feel hurt or defensive if I think something I did is being misunderstood, but I don’t think I’m usually chasing admiration.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a consistent pattern of manipulative behavior

patient.answer:

Charm is a little harder, because I work with people, and I can be diplomatic. I try to phrase things in a way that people can hear, and I may try to smooth things over or make a case for something. But I don’t think of that as charm in a calculated way. It’s more like trying to communicate effectively, or trying not to make a situation worse.

I guess if I want something, I can be persuasive. I can explain why I think it makes sense, and I probably keep talking longer than I need to sometimes. But I’m not aware of using people, or flattering them just to get my way, or pretending to be someone I’m not so they’ll agree with me.

So, no, I haven’t really noticed that in myself. If other people experience me that way, I suppose I’d want to know, but from the inside it doesn’t feel like I’m manipulating people.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a consistent pattern of impulsivity in their decisions
doctor.question: Do you often act on impulse without fully considering the consequences of your actions?

target_item.name: Painful_Consequence_Behavior
target_item.manifestation: I'm here because I pushed ahead with the onboarding launch and committed company money and vendor time before approvals were in place, and at the time it felt bold and necessary but now I'm on leave and everyone is asking what I was thinking.
target_item.reason: The question asks about acting impulsively without fully considering consequences, which directly matches excessive involvement in risky activities with painful consequences.

patient.answer:
Yes… I mean, I don’t like saying “often,” because I don’t think I’m impulsive in every part of my life. I’m not usually someone who just does reckless things for no reason. But if you’re asking whether I acted without fully thinking through the consequences in the situation that brought me here, then yes. I think I have to say yes.

The clearest example is the onboarding launch. I pushed ahead with it before all the approvals were actually in place. At the time it didn’t feel impulsive to me. That’s the strange part. It felt bold, decisive, necessary — like if I waited for every sign-off and every committee discussion, the whole thing would lose momentum and everyone would later agree I had been right to move it forward.

But looking back, I committed company money and vendor time before I really had the authority to do that. I can say now that I did not sit with the consequences properly. I didn’t really think through what would happen if leadership didn’t back me, or if finance objected, or if the vendor started work and then people asked who approved it. I sort of assumed the outcome would justify the decision.

And now I’m on leave, and everyone is basically asking, “What were you thinking?” Which is painful, because at the time I thought I was solving a problem, not creating one. So yes, in that situation, I acted first and understood the consequences later.

doctor.intent: To determine if the patient has a grandiose sense of self-importance
doctor.question: Do you often feel entitled to special treatment or automatic obedience from others because of your intelligence, talent, or accomplishments?

target_item.reason: The question is about entitlement to special treatment or automatic obedience, which is not covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I feel entitled to special treatment, no. At least, I don’t walk around thinking rules shouldn’t apply to me because I’m smart or because I’ve done good work. That sounds ugly when I say it that way, and I really don’t believe that’s how I usually see myself.

I do think I get frustrated when I feel like people aren’t listening to reason, or when a process seems slow or overly cautious. And maybe in those moments I can come across as if I think my judgment should carry more weight than everyone else’s. I can see that possibility. But from the inside, it doesn’t feel like, “I’m special, so obey me.” It feels more like, “I’ve thought this through, why are we getting stuck?”

Automatic obedience… no, that doesn’t sound right. I don’t expect people to just follow me blindly. I actually prefer when people understand the reasoning. I can get impatient when they don’t, or when I think the objections are more procedural than substantive, but that’s different from expecting obedience because of who I am.

So I guess my answer is: not usually, no. I may overestimate how obvious my reasoning is, or feel offended if my competence is questioned, but I don’t think I generally believe I deserve special treatment just because of my intelligence or accomplishments.

doctor.intent: To determine if the patient has a consistent pattern of grandiosity
doctor.question: Do you often feel like your opinions or ideas are more valuable or important than those of others?

target_item.reason: The question is about believing my opinions or ideas are more valuable than others', which is not directly covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly. I mean, I do have opinions, and when I’ve thought something through carefully, I can feel pretty convinced that I’m right. Sometimes probably too convinced, if I’m being honest. But “more valuable or important than other people’s” sounds like I’m dismissing everyone else as irrelevant, and I don’t think that’s how I generally operate.

I usually want to hear what other people think, especially if they have information I don’t have. I can get frustrated, though, when I feel like an idea is being rejected for reasons that don’t seem substantive to me, or when the conversation feels like it’s going in circles. Then I might push harder and talk too much, and I can see how that might make it seem like I think my view matters more.

From the inside, it feels less like “my ideas are inherently better” and more like, “I believe this particular idea makes sense, and I’m trying to get people to see why.” But I guess the effect can still be that I crowd out other people’s perspectives. I don’t like that possibility, but I can recognize it.

So… not as a general belief, no. I don’t think my opinions are automatically more important just because they’re mine. But when I’m convinced of something, I may act like they are more important in that moment, even if I don’t mean to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pattern of taking advantage of others to achieve their own ends
doctor.question: Have you ever taken advantage of someone's trust or naivety for your own gain?

target_item.reason: The question asks about exploiting someone’s trust or naivety for personal gain, which is not covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
No… I don’t think so. At least, not in the sense of deliberately looking at someone and thinking, “They trust me, so I can use that.” That would feel really awful to me.

I’ve definitely benefited from people trusting me at work — people assuming I know what I’m doing, giving me room to make decisions, not questioning every little thing — but I don’t think I’ve consciously exploited that for personal gain. And “naivety” especially… I don’t think I target people who are less experienced or easier to persuade. I mean, I hope I don’t.

I suppose there may have been times when I was persuasive and got people to go along with something because I believed I was right, and maybe they trusted my judgment more than they should have. But that’s different, at least in my mind, from taking advantage of them. I wasn’t trying to get something out of them for myself.

So my answer would be no, not that I’m aware of. If someone else felt used by me, I’d want to know that, but I don’t recognize that as a pattern in myself.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a grandiose sense of self-importance
doctor.question: Do you generally believe you are more capable of making important decisions than most other people?

target_item.reason: The question asks about a general belief of superior decision-making ability, which relates to grandiosity or self-importance, but this symptom profile does not include a specific item covering that belief.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I generally believe that, no. I mean, “important decisions” is a big category. If it’s something in an area I know well, or something where I’ve really done the work and looked at the consequences, then yes, I might trust my judgment more than I trust the average off-the-cuff opinion. But that’s not the same as thinking I’m more capable than most people across the board.

I work with people, so I see all the time that different people are good at different kinds of decisions. Some people are better at reading the emotional side of a situation, some are better at legal or procedural details, some are better at stepping back when things get heated. I don’t think I’m superior at all of that. If anything, I can sometimes get too locked into what seems logical to me and miss that someone else is seeing a different piece of the picture.

That said, I probably do have a lot of confidence in my own reasoning when I feel informed. Maybe more confidence than is always helpful. I can think, “Why are we overcomplicating this?” or “This seems obvious,” and then later realize it wasn’t obvious to everyone because they were weighing things differently. So I guess I’d say I trust myself, sometimes strongly, but I don’t walk around believing I’m inherently better than most people at making major decisions.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a pattern of grandiosity
doctor.question: Do you often find yourself exaggerating your achievements or talents to others?

patient.answer:
I don’t think I often exaggerate, no. I mean… I might present things in the best light, especially at work, because that’s sort of part of how people talk about accomplishments. Like if I’ve led a project, I’ll say I led it, but I try not to make it sound like I single-handedly did everything if other people were involved.

I’m actually a little careful about that, because in HR you hear people describe their performance or their conflict with someone, and you can tell when they’re inflating their role or leaving out context. So I’m conscious of not wanting to be that person. At least, I hope I’m not.

That said, I probably do emphasize the parts I’m proud of. If I’m in an interview-type situation or trying to explain why I handled something well, I might highlight my judgment or experience. But I don’t think I invent achievements or claim talents I don’t have. I’d be too worried about being caught out, honestly, and it would feel embarrassing.

So… not often, I’d say. Maybe I polish the wording sometimes, but I don’t see myself as someone who exaggerates in a major way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a grandiose sense of self-importance
doctor.question: Do you often feel like you deserve special treatment because of your accomplishments or status?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about entitlement or expecting special treatment due to accomplishments/status, which is not covered by the listed bipolar symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think so, not in a broad sense. I mean, I think everyone likes to be recognized for work they’ve done, and I’m not immune to that. If I’ve put a lot into something and it goes well, I do appreciate people noticing, or at least not acting like it was nothing. But “special treatment” feels like a stronger thing.

I don’t think I walk into situations feeling like rules shouldn’t apply to me because of my job title or because I’ve accomplished certain things. If anything, because I work in HR, I’m pretty aware of how bad that looks — when someone thinks their seniority or reputation means they should get exceptions everyone else wouldn’t get. That kind of thing bothers me.

Now, I might expect a certain level of respect or professional courtesy, especially if I’ve earned trust over time. Like, if I’ve handled sensitive situations well before, I might feel frustrated if someone suddenly treats me like I don’t know what I’m doing. But I see that as wanting my experience to count for something, not wanting to be above other people.

I guess there are moments where I think, “Come on, I’ve been doing this long enough, I shouldn’t have to prove every little thing.” But I don’t think that’s the same as deserving special treatment. It’s more wanting not to be dismissed. So… no, I wouldn’t say I often feel that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a lack of empathy
doctor.question: Do you often have difficulty understanding why others are upset or offended by your actions?

target_item.reason: The question asks about difficulty understanding why others are upset or offended, which relates to empathy or social insight. The provided symptom profile does not directly cover this; the closest item involves high-risk behavior with consequences, but not specifically difficulty understanding others' reactions.

patient.answer:
I wouldn’t say often, no. I mean, I can usually understand it once someone explains what landed badly. Especially because of my work, I spend a lot of time thinking about tone, impact, how something might be received, whether someone felt dismissed or embarrassed. So it’s not like I’m completely oblivious to that kind of thing.

But there are definitely times where my first reaction is more like, “Wait, why did that upset you?” Not because I think they have no right to be upset, but because in my head I’m focused on the intent. Like if I was trying to solve a problem or be direct, I may not immediately see that the way I said it came across as critical or impatient. Then if they tell me, I can usually back up and say, okay, I can see how that sounded.

I think I’m better at understanding it after the fact than in the moment. In the moment, I might be a little too caught up in the practical side — what needs to happen, what decision needs to be made, what the policy is, that sort of thing. And then later I’ll replay it and realize, “Oh, they weren’t reacting to the content, they were reacting to feeling talked over,” or something like that.

So… difficulty, sometimes. Often, I don’t think so. I’m not always as quick as I’d like to be, but I usually can get there if I slow down or if the person tells me directly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a lack of empathy
doctor.question: Do you find it hard to put yourself in other people's shoes and understand their feelings?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about empathy or difficulty understanding other people's feelings, which is not covered by the listed Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I find it hard in a general way, no. I mean, part of my job is almost literally trying to understand where different people are coming from, even when they’re upset or when I don’t personally agree with them. I have to think about, okay, what did this feel like from their side, what might they be worried about, are they feeling disrespected, embarrassed, threatened, ignored — all of that.

That said, I’m probably better at doing it when I have time to step back and think. In the moment, especially if things are tense or someone is being emotional in a way that feels unfair to me, I can get a little too focused on the facts. Like, “Here’s what happened, here’s the policy, here’s what I meant,” and I may not immediately slow down enough to really sit with how it felt for them. Later, I can usually see it more clearly.

So I wouldn’t say I’m unable to put myself in someone else’s shoes. I do care how people feel, and I can usually understand it if I stop and think or if they tell me directly. But I’m not perfect at it in real time. Sometimes I need a minute to get out of my own perspective first.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a lack of empathy
doctor.question: Do you think you have trouble understanding and sharing the feelings of others?

target_item.reason: The question is about empathy—understanding and sharing others' feelings—which is not covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I mean… I’m not sure I’d describe it as trouble understanding or sharing feelings, at least not as a general pattern. I do try to understand what other people are feeling, and I don’t think I’m cold to it. If someone is upset in front of me, I usually do care, even if I’m also trying to figure out what actually happened or what needs to be done.

I guess where I hesitate is the “sharing” part, because I don’t always feel things in the same way someone else does. Like, I can understand that someone feels hurt or embarrassed or anxious without necessarily feeling it right along with them. Sometimes I’m more analytical at first — I’m thinking, okay, what led to this, what can I do, what do they need from me — and then the emotional part catches up a little later.

So… not usually, no. But I can be slower with it in the moment than I’d like. If I’m stressed or trying to solve something, I may come across more practical than warm, and I can see how someone might experience that as me not getting it. I don’t think that means I don’t understand or care, but I probably don’t always show it right away.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a lack of empathy
doctor.question: Do you usually consider how your actions might affect the feelings of others before you do something?

target_item.reason: The question asks about routinely considering how actions affect other people's feelings before acting, which relates to empathy or social awareness. The provided symptom profile does not include a specific item covering this.

patient.answer:
Usually, yes — or at least I try to. I think I probably consider it more in some settings than others. At work, for example, I’m very aware that what I say or how I say it can affect people. If I’m sending an email, having a difficult conversation, giving feedback, dealing with a complaint, I’ll often think through how it might land. Like, will this make the person feel blamed, or cornered, or dismissed? Am I being clear without sounding harsh? That kind of thing.

In my personal life, I do think about it too, but maybe not always as deliberately. If I’m tired or focused on getting something done, I can be more blunt than I intend, and I may not fully think through the emotional impact until afterward. Then I’ll sort of replay it and think, “Okay, that may have sounded sharper than I meant,” or “I probably should’ve said that differently.”

So I wouldn’t say I go around not caring how people feel. I do care. But I’m not always perfect at anticipating it before I act. Sometimes I’m better at recognizing it after the fact, especially if someone reacts strongly or tells me directly.

doctor.intent: To determine if the patient has a consistent pattern of manipulating others for personal gain, which could help differentiate between the candidate diagnoses of F60.0, F60.2, and F60.3

patient.answer:
I’m trying to think how to answer that honestly, because “position or influence” can mean a lot of things. In my work, technically I do have some influence in situations — not like I’m the final authority on everything, but people may take what I say seriously because of my role. So I’m pretty aware that I have to be careful with that.

Have I used it for my own benefit? I don’t think so, not in a manipulative way. I mean, I’ve probably advocated for something that made my life easier, like suggesting a process or pushing for a decision that I thought would reduce problems later, including problems for me. But I wouldn’t say I’ve pressured someone or taken advantage of my role to get something personal out of it.

If you mean something like steering someone’s decision so I get a favor, or avoid consequences, or get special treatment — no, I don’t think that’s something I do. I’d actually be pretty uncomfortable with that, because in HR especially, that kind of thing can get unethical very quickly. I’m sure I have opinions and biases like anyone does, but I try not to use my role that way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a lack of empathy
doctor.question: Do you often find it difficult to understand why someone would feel a certain way in a situation?

target_item.reason: The doctor's question is about difficulty understanding others' emotions or empathic perspective-taking, which is not covered by the provided Bipolar I symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Not often, no. I mean, I can usually come up with a reason why someone might feel the way they do, even if I wouldn’t feel the same way in that exact situation. A lot of the time it’s kind of… I look at the circumstances, what the person values, what they might be afraid of, what history might be there, and then it makes sense enough.

There are times I don’t get it right away, though. Especially if someone has what seems to me like a very intense reaction to something I would see as minor, or if they don’t explain what part of it upset them. Then I might think, “Wait, why is this such a big deal?” But usually if I slow down and ask a few questions, or think about it from their angle, I can understand it better.

So I wouldn’t say it’s a frequent difficulty. It’s more that sometimes my first reaction is practical or logical, and the emotional reasoning takes a minute to catch up. But I’m not usually just baffled by other people’s feelings.
